content: 1. Diagnosing appendicitis in young children can be particularly challenging. Symptoms may include fever, anorexia, and variable vomiting. The pain often begins around the periumbilical region but progresses to persistent pain and tenderness in the right lower quadrant, which is the most critical clinical finding. 2. A raised white blood cell count can aid in the diagnosis of appendicitis. Ultrasound examination performed by a skilled observer is also highly beneficial. 3. In cases of suspected appendicitis, the child should be kept nil by mouth, and intravenous fluids should be administered. If the child is in shock, administer a rapid IV bolus of 20 mL/kg of normal saline or Hartmann’s solution. If shock persists, repeat the bolus while monitoring for circulatory fluid overload. For dehydration without shock, administer 10–20 mL/kg of half-strength Darrow’s solution or normal saline with 5% glucose over 20 minutes. 4. Antibiotics such as ceftriaxone (5 mg/kg IM or IV once daily) and metronidazole (10 mg/kg three times daily) should be given if there are signs of infection, such as fever or peritonitis. 5. An urgent review by a pediatric surgeon is essential. Appendectomy should be performed as soon as possible to prevent complications like perforation, peritonitis, or abscess formation. It is better to operate and be wrong about the diagnosis than to delay and risk peritonitis. 6. Bowel obstruction presents differently depending on the level of obstruction. Proximal obstruction typically causes vomiting with minimal abdominal distension, while distal obstruction leads to significant distension and delayed vomiting. Symptoms often include cramping abdominal pain, distension, and absence of flatus. Visible peristalsis waves may sometimes be observed, and abdominal X-rays often reveal distended bowel loops with air-fluid levels. 7. In cases of bowel obstruction, the child should be kept nil by mouth, and fluid resuscitation should be initiated. Correct shock, if present, with a rapid IV bolus of 20 mL/kg of normal saline or Hartmann’s solution. If the child is dehydrated but not in shock, administer 10–20 mL/kg of half-strength Darrow’s solution or normal saline with 5% glucose over 20 minutes. A nasogastric tube should be passed to relieve nausea, vomiting, and prevent bowel perforation. 8. Intussusception, a form of bowel obstruction where one segment of the intestine telescopes into another, most commonly occurs at the ileocecal junction. It typically affects children under 2 years of age but can occur in older children. Early symptoms include colicky abdominal pain and vomiting, with the child crying in pain, doubling over, and pulling their legs up. Late symptoms include pallor, abdominal distension, tenderness, bloody diarrhea (often described as red currant jelly stool), and dehydration. A palpable abdominal mass may be present. 9. Treatment for intussusception involves urgent review by a pediatric surgeon. If air or barium enema reduction fails, surgery is required. If the bowel is ischemic or necrotic, resection is necessary. Transfer the patient to a facility with experienced personnel and appropriate imaging if needed. 10. Umbilical hernias are diagnosed by the presence of a soft, reducible swelling at the umbilicus. Most close spontaneously, but surgical repair is recommended if the hernia persists beyond 6 years of age or if it is difficult to reduce. 11. Inguinal hernias present as intermittent, reducible swelling in the groin, often observed when the child is crying or straining. They occur at the site where the spermatic cord exits the abdomen. Distinguishing from a hydrocele is important, as hydroceles transilluminate and do not extend into the inguinal canal. Uncomplicated inguinal hernias require elective surgical repair to prevent incarceration. Hydroceles that do not resolve by 1 year of age should also be repaired. 12. Testicular torsion causes acute swelling and severe pain in one side of the scrotum. The testis is extremely tender. Urgent surgical intervention is required to preserve the testis, with a high success rate if performed within 6 hours. 13. Rectal prolapse, often associated with chronic diarrhea and poor nutrition, occurs during defecation. Initially, the prolapsed section reduces spontaneously but may later require manual reduction. Complications include bleeding or strangulation with gangrene. Treatment involves gentle manual reduction, addressing underlying causes of diarrhea and malnutrition, and treating parasitic infections if present. Recurrent prolapse may require surgical intervention, such as a Thiersch stitch. 14. Abscesses are collections of pus caused by infection. Symptoms include fever, swelling, tenderness, and a fluctuant mass. Treatment involves incision and drainage, which may require general anesthesia for large abscesses. Antibiotics like cloxacillin (25–50 mg/kg four times daily) are given for 5 days or until surrounding cellulitis resolves. 15. Osteomyelitis, an infection of the bone, often results from hematogenous spread or open fractures. Acute osteomyelitis presents with bone pain, tenderness, intermittent fever, and refusal to move the affected limb or bear weight. Early X-rays may be normal, with changes appearing after 12–14 days. Chronic osteomyelitis involves draining sinuses and X-ray findings of elevated periosteum and sequestrum. Treatment includes antibiotics (e.g., chloramphenicol or cloxacillin) and surgical debridement if necessary. 16. Septic arthritis involves joint infection, presenting with pain and swelling. Joint aspiration under sterile conditions confirms the diagnosis. Urgent surgical washout is required to prevent joint destruction. Antibiotics like chloramphenicol or cloxacillin are administered based on the child’s age and clinical condition. 17. Pyomyositis is characterized by pus within a muscle, often in the thigh. Symptoms include fever, tenderness, and swelling. Incision and drainage are required, with a drain left in place for 2–3 days. X-rays should be performed to rule out underlying osteomyelitis. Antibiotics like cloxacillin are given for 5–10 days. 18. Supportive care in pediatric wards includes effective communication with parents, prioritizing care for critically ill children, ensuring comfort and pain control, preventing hospital-acquired infections, and maintaining a warm environment for young or malnourished children to prevent hypothermia. 19. Breastfeeding is crucial for infant health and recovery. Exclusive breastfeeding is recommended for the first 6 months, with continued breastfeeding alongside complementary foods until at least 2 years of age. Health workers should support mothers in overcoming breastfeeding challenges, such as insufficient milk supply, by encouraging frequent suckling and skin-to-skin contact.
